heroText: Nuuk is a Greenland base best planned around named sights rather than a generic stopover. Start with Nuuk fjord, add Greenland National Museum, and use Katuaq to understand the city's history, street life and visitor rhythm. Nuuk International Airport handles the main arrival flow, so hotel choice should balance the centre, transfer time and day-trip plans.

history.label: Origins
history.text: Early settlement The site has a long history of habitation.

history.label: 2200 BCE
history.text: The area around Nuuk was first occupied by the ancient, pre-Inuit, Paleo-Eskimo people of the Saqqaq culture as far back as 2200 BCE, when they lived in the area around the now abandoned settlement.
For a long time, it was occupied by the Dorset culture around the former settlement of Kangeq, but they disappeared from the Nuuk district before 1000 AD.

history.label: 15th century
history.text: The Nuuk area was then inhabited by Norse settlers from around 1000 until the disappearance of the settlement for uncertain reasons during the 15th century.

The city proper was founded as the fort of Godt-Haab in 1728 by the royal governor Claus Paarss, when he relocated the missionary and merchant Hans Egede's earlier Hope Colony (Haabets Koloni) from Kangeq.
Hans Egede returned to Denmark in 1736 after 15 years in Greenland, leaving his son Poul to continue his work.
In response, in 1861, he started the Atuagagdliutit, Greenland's first newspaper, with a native Greenlander as editor.

From this base, further missions were established at Lichtenfels (1748), Lichtenau (1774), Friedrichsthal (1824), Umanak (1861), and Idlorpait (1864), before they were discontinued in 1900 and folded into the Lutheran Church of Denmark. Cultural.

Godthaab became the seat of government for the Danish colony of South Greenland, while Godhavn (modern Qeqertarsuaq) was the capital of North Greenland until 1940, when the administration was unified in Godthaab. Missionary settlements.
Under new regulations in 1950, two councils amalgamated into one.
This Countryside Council was abolished on 1 May 1979, when the Greenland Home Rule government renamed the city of Godthåb to Nuuk.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: This became the nucleus of present-day Nuuk as many Greenlanders from the southeastern coast left their territory to live at the mission station.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: This newspaper based in Nuuk later became an important token of Greenlandic identity. World War II and postwar changes During World War II, there was a reawakening of Greenlandic national identity.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: By proportion and by cultural authority and impact, it may well be tiny Nuuk that is the most indigenous city in the world.
